name: Micaiah the son of Imlah
charge: As the Lord liveth, what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak: against four hundred prophets, two kings, a slap, and a prison
summary: When Ahab and Jehoshaphat sat on their thrones at the gate of Samaria and four hundred prophets told them with one voice to go up to Ramoth-gilead, Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord, and Ahab named Micaiah and said he hated him because he never prophesied good concerning him (1 Kings 22:6-8). Coached to agree with the others, Micaiah answered that he would speak only what the Lord told him, saw Israel scattered like sheep without a shepherd and a lying spirit in the mouths of the four hundred, and was struck and imprisoned on short rations (1 Kings 22:13-27). He staked his word on the outcome, and Ahab did not come back (1 Kings 22:28-38).
offenseFull: After three years without war, Jehoshaphat king of Judah came down to Ahab, who wanted Ramoth-gilead back from the king of Syria; Jehoshaphat agreed to go, but first asked that they inquire at the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:1-5). Ramoth-gilead, a Levitical city of refuge east of the Jordan, had been lost to Aram-Damascus. Ahab gathered about four hundred prophets, and they all said go up, the Lord would deliver it into the king’s hand (1 Kings 22:6). After the split the northern kingdom fell into idolatry and forsook the Levites, and a prophet of the Most High wanted nothing to do with their manner of worship, as Elisha later told a king of Israel to go to the prophets of his father and mother (2 Kings 3:13). Jehoshaphat saw something in the spirit: four hundred men agreeing was not the counsel of God, and he asked whether there was not a prophet of the Lord besides (1 Kings 22:7).

Ahab said there was one more, Micaiah the son of Imlah, but he hated him, because he never prophesied good concerning him, only evil (1 Kings 22:8). The teaching presses the point: Ahab already knew where true counsel was, and chose four hundred who would tell him what he wanted to hear. He called the counsel of God evil because it went against his flesh. They acknowledged the spirit of the Lord was on Micaiah and hated him for the words of the law that came out of his mouth; he did not preach what they wanted, and they did not like it. The messenger sent to fetch him tried to prepare him: all the prophets spoke good to the king with one voice, so let his word be like theirs (1 Kings 22:13). In plain terms, lie to the king and make it sound good. Micaiah swore by the living Lord that whatever the Lord said to him, that he would speak (1 Kings 22:14). To the law and to the testimony: if they do not speak according to that word, there is no light in them (Isaiah 8:20).

At first he answered the king in the words of the others, until Ahab demanded the truth in the name of the Lord, wanting to be told the truth and lied to at the same time. Then Micaiah said he saw all Israel scattered on the hills like sheep with no shepherd, and the Lord said they had no master and should go home in peace (1 Kings 22:15-17). It was counsel to save Ahab’s life, and mercy from God, and Ahab heard it as evil. Micaiah told him the rest: he saw the Lord on His throne with the host of heaven on either side, and a spirit offered to go and speak lies through all Ahab’s prophets, and the Lord sent it (1 Kings 22:19-23). The deceived and the deceiver both belong to Him (Job 12:16), and it is the Lord’s counsel that stands (Proverbs 19:21).
judgmentFull: Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah struck Micaiah on the cheek, and Ahab had him taken to Amon the governor and Joash the king’s son, to be kept in prison on the bread and water of affliction until the king came back in peace (1 Kings 22:24-27). They put him in prison because they did not like what he spoke; not for adultery, not for striking a brother, not for stealing. His light shone on their darkness, and roaches scatter when the light turns on. Micaiah answered that if the king came back in peace at all, the Lord had not spoken by him, and called all the people to hear it (1 Kings 22:28).

Ahab disguised himself for the battle and had Jehoshaphat wear his robes. The Syrian captains chased Jehoshaphat and turned back when they saw he was not the king of Israel, and a man drew his bow at random and struck Ahab between the joints of his armor. God makes no mistakes; when the counsel of the Lord is rejected, judgment finds its mark. Ahab died at evening, and the dogs licked his blood when the chariot was washed at the pool of Samaria, according to the word of the Lord (1 Kings 22:29-38). The four hundred were exposed by the test the law gives: when the thing does not come to pass, the Lord has not spoken it (Deuteronomy 18:22). The record does not say Micaiah was released; his vindication did not depend on his comfort. He was not afraid of four hundred men, and that is how we must be; Christ said not to be ashamed of him, and the same hatred falls today on those who speak the laws.

text.text: Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, about four hundred men, and said unto them, Shall I go against Ramoth–gilead to battle, or shall I forbear? And they said, Go up; for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king.
And Jehoshaphat said, Is there not here a prophet of the Lord besides, that we might enquire of him?

And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, There is yet one man, Micaiah the son of Imlah, by whom we may enquire of the Lord: but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil. And Jehoshaphat said, Let not the king say so.

And the messenger that was gone to call Micaiah spake unto him, saying, Behold now, the words of the prophets declare good unto the king with one mouth: let thy word, I pray thee, be like the word of one of them, and speak that which is good.
And Micaiah said, As the Lord liveth, what the Lord saith unto me, that will I speak.

So he came to the king. And the king said unto him, Micaiah, shall we go against Ramoth–gilead to battle, or shall we forbear? And he answered him, Go, and prosper: for the Lord shall deliver it into the hand of the king.
And the king said unto him, How many times shall I adjure thee that thou tell me nothing but that which is true in the name of the Lord?
And he said, I saw all Israel scattered upon the hills, as sheep that have not a shepherd: and the Lord said, These have no master: let them return every man to his house in peace.
And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, Did I not tell thee that he would prophesy no good concerning me, but evil?
And he said, Hear thou therefore the word of the Lord: I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left.
And the Lord said, Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth–gilead? And one said on this manner, and another said on that manner.
And there came forth a spirit, and stood before the Lord, and said, I will persuade him.

And the Lord said unto him, Wherewith? And he said, I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so.
Now therefore, behold, the Lord hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets, and the Lord hath spoken evil concerning thee.
But Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah went near, and smote Micaiah on the cheek, and said, Which way went the Spirit of the Lord from me to speak unto thee?
And Micaiah said, Behold, thou shalt see in that day, when thou shalt go into an inner chamber to hide thyself.
And the king of Israel said, Take Micaiah, and carry him back unto Amon the governor of the city, and to Joash the king’s son;
And say, Thus saith the king, Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I come in peace.
And Micaiah said, If thou return at all in peace, the Lord hath not spoken by me. And he said, Hearken, O people, every one of you.
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth–gilead.
And the king of Israel said unto Jehoshaphat, I will disguise myself, and enter into the battle; but put thou on thy robes. And the king of Israel disguised himself, and went into the battle.
But the king of Syria commanded his thirty and two captains that had rule over his chariots, saying, Fight neither with small nor great, save only with the king of Israel.
And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, that they said, Surely it is the king of Israel. And they turned aside to fight against him: and Jehoshaphat cried out.
And it came to pass, when the captains of the chariots perceived that it was not the king of Israel, that they turned back from pursuing him.

And a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel between the joints of the harness: wherefore he said unto the driver of his chariot, Turn thine hand, and carry me out of the host; for I am wounded.
And the battle increased that day: and the king was stayed up in his chariot against the Syrians, and died at even: and the blood ran out of the wound into the midst of the chariot.
And there went a proclamation throughout the host about the going down of the sun, saying, Every man to his city, and every man to his own country.
So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria.
And one washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood; and they washed his armour; according unto the word of the Lord which he spake.
And they continued three years without war between Syria and Israel.
And it came to pass in the third year, that Jehoshaphat the king of Judah came down to the king of Israel.
And the king of Israel said unto his servants, Know ye that Ramoth in Gilead is ours, and we be still, and take it not out of the hand of the king of Syria?
And he said unto Jehoshaphat, Wilt thou go with me to battle to Ramoth–gilead? And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, I am as thou art, my people as thy people, my horses as thy horses.
And Jehoshaphat said unto the king of Israel, Enquire, I pray thee, at the word of the Lord to day.
